subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Diesel vs. Gasoline
description: A 60-second lesson on Diesel vs. Gasoline.

hook.text: Diesel engines have no spark plugs. The fuel ignites purely from the heat of heavy compression.

buildup.text: Rudolf Diesel's original 1893 design compressed air so hard it got hot enough to ignite fuel on contact.

discovery.text: Diesels are more efficient—about 40% thermal efficiency compared to 30% for gasoline engines.

twist.text: But they produce more nitrogen oxides and soot. Cleaning that up requires expensive aftertreatment systems.

climax.text: After Dieselgate, many countries are phasing out diesel passenger cars entirely.

punchline.text: Diesel is more efficient but harder to keep clean.

quiz.question: How does diesel fuel ignite in the engine?

details.summary: Diesel engines compress air until it is hot enough to ignite fuel without a spark, producing more torque and better fuel economy than gasoline engines but generating more nitrogen oxide emissions.
details.whyItMatters: The diesel-versus-gasoline choice affects fuel costs, emissions, and driving feel. Understanding the trade-offs helps drivers and policymakers make informed energy decisions.
takeaways: Diesel engines use compression ignition rather than spark plugs
They produce more torque at low RPMs, ideal for towing
Diesel emits less CO2 per mile but more NOx and particulates

faq.question: Why are diesel cars more popular in Europe than in America?
faq.answer: European fuel taxes historically made diesel cheaper per mile. Longer highway distances and diesel's superior fuel economy made it the preferred European choice, though that trend is reversing post-Dieselgate.

faq.question: Is diesel being phased out?
faq.answer: Many cities are banning older diesels from central zones, and several countries plan to end new diesel car sales. However, diesel remains important for trucks and heavy machinery where torque is critical.
